text: In the CIA triad, what does confidentiality protect?
choices: Information from unauthorized disclosure
Systems from every possible outage
Data from every accidental change
Networks from physical damage

text: In the CIA triad, what does integrity protect?
choices: Information from being viewed by anyone
Information from unauthorized alteration
Servers from running out of electricity
Users from forgetting passwords

text: In the CIA triad, what does availability concern?
choices: Keeping every file secret from its owner
Preventing all changes to a database
Authorized users being able to access a service when needed
Proving who wrote a software package

text: What does authentication establish?
choices: The files a user may open
The cost of an incident
The encryption algorithm in a certificate
The identity of a user or system

text: What does authorization determine after a user is authenticated?
choices: Which resources and actions that identity may use
Whether the identity exists at all
Whether a packet has an IP address
How a password is hashed

text: What is multi-factor authentication designed to require?
choices: Two passwords from the same list
Two or more different factor types
Two accounts on the same device
Two antivirus products

text: What is phishing?
choices: A scan that checks disk sectors
A protocol for encrypting Wi-Fi
A deceptive message intended to trick a recipient
A backup stored on tape

text: What makes spear phishing different from broad phishing?
choices: It uses only telephone calls
It attacks only wireless networks
It is always sent by a trusted employee
It targets a particular person or organization with tailored content

text: What is malware?
choices: Software designed to perform harmful or unauthorized actions
Any software that has a graphical interface
A tool used only to compress files
A physical cable used for networking

text: What is ransomware typically designed to do?
choices: Improve the speed of a database
Deny access to data or systems and demand payment
Issue certificates to websites
Route packets between subnets

text: Why is timely security patching important?
choices: It guarantees that no future flaw can exist
It replaces every user password automatically
It fixes known flaws that attackers may exploit
It makes encrypted data readable

text: What does the principle of least privilege grant?
choices: Every administrator every possible permission
Anonymous access to public and private data
A separate password for every network packet
Only the access needed for an authorized task

text: What is defense in depth?
choices: Using multiple complementary security controls
Placing all protection at a single firewall
Encrypting only files that are already public
Removing logging to reduce system load

text: What is the primary function of a network firewall?
choices: Generate random passwords for employees
Permit or block traffic according to defined rules
Repair corrupted hard-drive sectors
Convert domain names into certificates

text: What does an intrusion detection system generally do?
choices: Automatically encrypt every database
Assign IP addresses to new devices
Detect and alert on suspicious activity
Replace a router's operating system

text: What distinguishes an intrusion prevention system from a passive IDS?
choices: It cannot inspect network traffic
It is used only for password storage
It operates only when a system is offline
It can take configured action to block or disrupt detected traffic

text: What is a vulnerability?
choices: A weakness that could be exploited
A confirmed criminal identity
A backup that has passed a restore test
A packet that has completed routing

text: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
choices: A flaw that can be exploited only at midnight
A newly disclosed or exploited flaw with no established vendor fix available
A vulnerability in a system with zero users
A patch that was released zero days ago

text: Why are offline or immutable backups valuable against ransomware?
choices: They make every workstation immune to phishing
They eliminate the need to test restoration
They are harder for the same attack to encrypt or delete
They allow anyone to bypass authentication

text: What is encryption primarily used to provide?
choices: Availability by adding more network bandwidth
Integrity by deleting old versions
Authentication by assigning an IP address
Confidentiality by transforming readable data into protected ciphertext

text: What key arrangement does symmetric encryption use?
choices: The same secret key, or a shared secret, for encryption and decryption
A public key only for both operations
A different public key for every byte
No key because the algorithm is one-way

text: What key arrangement does public-key encryption use?
choices: One password copied to every recipient
A mathematically related public key and private key
A hash value and a salt only
Two identical secret keys printed in plaintext

text: What is a cryptographic hash intended to produce?
choices: A reversible copy of the original file
A routable network address
A fixed-length digest of input data
A human-readable encryption password

text: Why is a unique salt added when storing a password hash?
choices: It lets a server recover the original password
It replaces the need for a slow password KDF
It allows the password to be sent in plaintext
It makes identical passwords produce different stored hashes and frustrates precomputed tables

text: What can a valid digital signature help a recipient verify?
choices: The message's integrity and association with the signer's private key
That the message is confidential without encryption
That the sender has administrator access
That the network route was shortest

text: What security property does HTTPS add to ordinary HTTP?
choices: A guarantee that the website contains no malware
TLS protection for the connection, including encryption and server authentication
A faster DNS resolver
A replacement for user authorization

text: What is DNS primarily used to do?
choices: Encrypt files on a workstation
Assign usernames to employees
Translate domain names into records such as IP addresses
Inspect executable code for viruses

text: What is DHCP primarily used to provide on a network?
choices: Digital signatures for email
A secure replacement for all web traffic
A database of password hashes
Automatic host configuration such as IP addresses and gateway information

text: What does an IP address identify at the network layer?
choices: A logical network location for an interface or host
The manufacturer password of a device
The cryptographic hash of a file
The physical length of a cable

text: What reliability feature is associated with TCP?
choices: No connection state and no retransmission
Ordered, acknowledged delivery with retransmission
Automatic end-to-end encryption
Name resolution for web domains

text: Why might an application choose UDP instead of TCP?
choices: It always guarantees delivery more strongly than TCP
It automatically authenticates every sender
It can avoid connection-oriented delivery overhead when the application handles loss or timing
It encrypts payloads without keys

text: In networking, what does a port number identify?
choices: The physical socket's voltage
A user's password age
A certificate's expiration date
A service or application endpoint on a host

text: What is a VPN intended to create over an untrusted network?
choices: An authenticated and encrypted tunnel between endpoints
A public copy of every internal database
A replacement for endpoint patching
A way to eliminate all routing

text: What is network segmentation?
choices: Replacing IP addresses with passwords
Dividing a network into zones with controlled communication between them
Putting every device on one unrestricted broadcast domain
Deleting logs at each router

text: What is a SIEM platform mainly used for?
choices: Compiling application source code
Issuing wireless channel licenses
Centralizing and correlating security events and logs
Storing only unencrypted passwords

text: In incident response, what is containment intended to accomplish first?
choices: Permanently prove the attacker's identity
Delete every affected disk immediately
Publish the incident before evidence is collected
Limit the incident's spread and ongoing damage

text: In disaster recovery, what does RTO measure?
choices: The target time to restore a service after disruption
The maximum tolerable data loss measured in time
The number of users in a recovery team
The strength of an encryption key

text: What is social engineering?
choices: Engineering a more efficient network cable
Manipulating people into revealing information or taking an unsafe action
Compressing social-media images
A mathematical proof of encryption strength

text: What is a brute-force password attack?
choices: Guessing a password from a public biography only
Changing a password after every login
Trying many candidate passwords until one succeeds
Hashing a password once with a random salt

text: What security objective is most directly threatened by a distributed denial-of-service attack?
choices: Confidentiality
Non-repudiation
Data minimization
Availability

text: What is SQL injection at a high level?
choices: Untrusted input changes the meaning of a database query
A database is encrypted with a symmetric key
A router drops packets with SQL text
A server stores passwords using a salt

text: What is cross-site scripting (XSS) at a high level?
choices: A browser refuses every valid certificate
Untrusted content causes a victim's browser to execute unintended script
A network switch duplicates an Ethernet frame
A database cannot accept a long password

text: What does a CSRF attack exploit in a browser session?
choices: A server's inability to calculate a hash
A firewall's lack of a public IP address
A victim's authenticated browser is induced to send an unwanted request
A certificate authority's use of elliptic curves

text: A database row is altered without authorization but remains available to users. Which CIA property was directly violated?
choices: Confidentiality
Availability
Authentication
Integrity

text: Which control is primarily preventive rather than detective?
choices: A firewall rule that blocks unauthorized inbound traffic
A report showing last month's login anomalies
A forensic image collected after an incident
An alert generated by a network sensor

text: What additional function is often represented by the third A in the AAA security model?
choices: Availability of a service
Accounting or auditing of actions
Asymmetric encryption
Address allocation

text: What does single sign-on (SSO) allow a user to do?
choices: Use one password without any identity verification
Bypass authorization in every application
Authenticate once and access multiple permitted applications
Encrypt all applications with one shared key

text: What is the primary distinction between OAuth 2.0 and an authentication protocol?
choices: OAuth is a disk-encryption algorithm
OAuth guarantees that every access token is permanent
OAuth replaces TLS for network confidentiality
OAuth is primarily an authorization delegation framework

text: What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
choices: An identity layer for authenticating the end user
A faster symmetric block cipher
A replacement for DNSSEC
A physical security token standard only

text: In SAML-based sign-in, what does an identity provider commonly issue to a service provider?
choices: A raw copy of the user's password
A signed assertion about the authenticated user
A DHCP lease for the service
A symmetric key printed in a URL

text: What does a Kerberos ticket primarily provide to a client?
choices: A permanent plaintext password for every service
A DNS record signed by a browser
A time-limited credential for requesting access to a service
A disk image used for backup restoration

text: Why are passkeys generally resistant to ordinary phishing websites?
choices: The user must type the same password twice
They transmit a reusable secret in every form
They work only when JavaScript is disabled
The credential is cryptographically bound to the legitimate site's origin

text: Which MFA method is generally considered more phishing-resistant?
choices: A FIDO2 security key
A code read from an email
A code sent by SMS
A static security question

text: What does role-based access control (RBAC) assign permissions through?
choices: The current weather at the user's location
Roles associated with users or groups
A separate encryption key for every file
Only the physical address of a device

text: What makes attribute-based access control (ABAC) more context-sensitive than simple RBAC?
choices: It removes all authorization decisions from policy
It permits access only to anonymous users
It evaluates attributes such as user, resource, action, and environment
It uses one role for every employee

text: What is privileged access management (PAM) intended to govern?
choices: Only public web-page styling
The physical temperature of a data center
Randomized names for ordinary files
High-impact administrator accounts and their use

text: What is a key security difference between a stateless ACL and a stateful firewall?
choices: A stateful firewall tracks connection context while a basic ACL evaluates each packet independently
A stateless ACL always encrypts traffic while a stateful firewall cannot
A stateful firewall assigns passwords while an ACL assigns usernames
A stateless ACL can inspect only files, not packets

text: What is the defensive purpose of endpoint detection and response (EDR)?
choices: Replace all network firewalls with antivirus signatures
Collect endpoint telemetry and support detection and investigation of suspicious behavior
Issue public certificates to laptops
Guarantee that an endpoint cannot be compromised

text: What does network detection and response (NDR) primarily analyze?
choices: Only the battery level of endpoint devices
The source code of every installed application
Network traffic and flow behavior for suspicious patterns
Physical access-card photographs

text: What is a honeypot in defensive security?
choices: A production database with no logging
A password shared by an incident team
A router configured to trust every host
A monitored decoy intended to attract or reveal unauthorized activity

text: Why is egress filtering useful in a network defense strategy?
choices: It restricts unauthorized outbound traffic and can limit data exfiltration
It makes inbound phishing messages impossible
It replaces identity verification at every application
It prevents every internal user from browsing the web

text: What is the central idea of a zero-trust security architecture?
choices: Every internal device is trusted permanently
Access is continuously evaluated rather than implicitly trusted because of network location
Only internet traffic requires authentication
A single perimeter firewall is sufficient

text: What does microsegmentation add beyond broad network segmentation?
choices: A requirement that all traffic use one shared password
A way to remove identity from access decisions
Fine-grained controls between individual workloads or small groups of workloads
A guarantee that lateral movement is impossible

text: What security problem does DNSSEC primarily address?
choices: It encrypts all DNS queries from observers
It replaces IP routing with public-key encryption
It prevents a domain owner from changing records
It authenticates DNS data so forged responses can be detected

text: What security property does mutual TLS (mTLS) add compared with server-authenticated TLS alone?
choices: Both sides present certificates and authenticate to each other
It removes the need for certificates on the server
It makes application authorization automatic
It uses only one shared password for all clients

text: What is the purpose of a certificate chain in a public-key infrastructure?
choices: It stores a user's plaintext password at every authority
It links an end-entity certificate to a trusted root through signed intermediates
It guarantees that a server's application is bug-free
It encrypts a file by concatenating certificates

text: What does perfect forward secrecy protect if a long-term server private key is later exposed?
choices: Every future session regardless of new key compromise
Passwords that were stored without hashing
Previously captured sessions that used independent ephemeral session keys
Traffic that was never encrypted

text: What does an AEAD construction provide together in one authenticated encryption operation?
choices: Password recovery and user authorization
DNS resolution and IP routing
Compression and deduplication without keys
Confidentiality and integrity for ciphertext, with authenticated associated data

text: Why is nonce reuse dangerous with many stream-like encryption modes?
choices: Reusing the same nonce can reveal relationships between plaintexts or undermine authenticity
It makes ciphertext longer than plaintext by definition
It automatically rotates the secret key too often
It prevents a recipient from knowing the sender's IP address

text: What type of flaw is a padding-oracle vulnerability associated with?
choices: A hash that has no possible collisions
A system that reveals whether decrypted block padding is valid
A certificate with too many trusted roots
A firewall that blocks every packet

text: Why are password-specific key derivation functions such as Argon2 deliberately expensive?
choices: They make passwords reversible for account recovery
They remove the need for unique salts
They increase the cost of testing large numbers of guesses
They guarantee that users will choose long passwords

text: What distinguishes a cryptographic hash collision from an ordinary repeated hash result?
choices: A collision requires that the same input be hashed twice
A collision occurs whenever a hash is salted
A collision means that encryption was successfully reversed
A collision means two distinct inputs produce the same digest

text: What does an HMAC combine to authenticate a message?
choices: A cryptographic hash with a shared secret key
A public certificate with no secret
Two unrelated plaintext passwords
A DNS query with an IP address only

text: Why does a digital signature not by itself provide message confidentiality?
choices: Signatures can be generated only from plaintext that is already encrypted
A signature authenticates or protects integrity but does not hide the signed message
A signature always uses a public key to decrypt the message
Confidentiality is impossible with public-key cryptography

text: What is the purpose of certificate revocation mechanisms such as CRLs or OCSP?
choices: To make an expired certificate valid again
To generate a private key from a public key
To signal that a certificate should no longer be trusted before its expiry
To encrypt DNS queries with a password

text: What is certificate transparency intended to make easier to detect?
choices: Weak passwords stored inside applications
Lost encryption keys on offline laptops
Unauthorized changes to private DNS zones only
Improperly issued public certificates through publicly auditable logs

text: Why is elliptic-curve cryptography often used instead of RSA at comparable security levels?
choices: It can provide comparable security with smaller keys
It uses no private key at all
It is a symmetric cipher with one universal secret
It makes certificate validation unnecessary

text: What is Diffie–Hellman key exchange designed to establish?
choices: A signed statement proving the sender's legal identity
A shared secret over a channel where the secret itself was not sent directly
A permanent password shared with every server
A hash collision between two messages

text: What does server-side request forgery (SSRF) cause a vulnerable server to do?
choices: Run script only in a visitor's browser
Hash a password with too few rounds
Make requests to unintended destinations using the server's network position
Sign a certificate without a private key

text: How does command injection differ from SQL injection?
choices: Command injection affects only certificates, while SQL injection affects only DNS
Command injection always requires a stolen password, while SQL injection never uses input
They are identical names for the same parser flaw
Command injection alters operating-system or interpreter commands, while SQL injection targets database queries

text: What does an XML external entity (XXE) vulnerability involve?
choices: Unsafe XML processing that permits unintended external entity resolution
A browser executing JavaScript from a trusted page
A router accepting an invalid MAC address
A hash function producing a short digest

text: What is path traversal?
choices: Moving laterally between network segments with a firewall rule
Using crafted path input to access files outside the intended directory
Walking through a certificate chain to a root authority
Converting an absolute IP address to a domain name

text: During incident response, what is eradication intended to accomplish?
choices: Temporarily isolate a host without changing it
Restore business services before evidence is considered
Remove the threat and its persistence from affected systems
Notify every external party before confirming scope

text: What is the main distinction between incident-response recovery and containment?
choices: Recovery always occurs before detection, while containment occurs after lessons learned
Recovery means deleting evidence, while containment means publishing it
They are two names for collecting volatile memory
Recovery returns systems to trusted operation after the threat is removed, while containment limits spread

text: Why is a synchronized incident timeline valuable to investigators?
choices: It helps correlate events across hosts and distinguish cause from consequence
It proves that every logged event was malicious
It makes timestamps independent of clock configuration
It replaces the need to preserve original evidence

text: What does CVSS primarily communicate about a vulnerability?
choices: A guarantee that exploitation is occurring in one organization
A standardized estimate of severity based on exploitability and impact factors
The exact number of vulnerable computers worldwide
A cryptographic proof that a patch is safe

text: Why should a high CVSS score not be treated as a complete remediation priority by itself?
choices: CVSS measures only password length
A high score means the flaw cannot be patched
Context such as asset exposure, active exploitation, and business impact also affects priority
CVSS applies only to physical locks

text: What is a supply-chain security risk in signed software updates?
choices: A user may forget to reboot after a patch
A firewall may block an unsigned web image
A public key may be shorter than a symmetric key
A trusted build or signing process could be compromised before distribution

text: Which evidence most strongly indicates credential stuffing rather than a conventional brute-force attack against one account?
choices: Many known username-password pairs are tried across many accounts with low attempts per account
One account receives millions of random guesses
A user enrolls a new hardware security key
A server rotates its TLS certificate

text: What distinguishes a replay attack from guessing a secret?
choices: An attacker invents a random password without observing traffic
An attacker reuses a previously captured valid message or credential
A defender rotates a key after an incident
A browser validates a server certificate

text: What defensive purpose does a nonce or sequence number serve in an authenticated protocol?
choices: It replaces the need for a secret key
It makes a hash reversible
It helps detect reuse or reordering of messages
It authorizes every user in a directory

text: What is the main security difference between a salted password hash and encrypted password storage?
choices: Encryption cannot use keys, while hashes always use public keys
A salt lets any user decrypt a password
They have exactly the same recovery properties
A properly designed password hash is intended to be one-way, while encryption is intended to be reversible with a key

text: What does authenticated associated data in an AEAD protocol allow?
choices: Metadata can remain unencrypted while still being integrity-protected
Metadata is automatically hidden without any encryption key
The recipient can change the ciphertext without detection
Associated data replaces the nonce

text: Why is certificate hostname validation essential even when a certificate chains to a trusted root?
choices: A trusted root guarantees that every hostname is covered
Trust also requires that the certificate identify the intended hostname
Hostname validation is needed only for symmetric ciphers
It proves that the site's application has no vulnerabilities

text: Why can an alert from a signature-based IDS miss a novel attack?
choices: Signatures can detect only physical theft
Novel attacks always use encrypted DNS
The attack may not match a known signature
An IDS cannot generate alerts from network traffic

text: What does behavioral detection attempt to identify?
choices: Only files whose names appear on a malware list
Only packets with invalid checksums
A user's legal authorization to work remotely
Activity that deviates from an established baseline or resembles suspicious behavior

text: Which design best limits lateral movement after one workload is compromised?
choices: Microsegmentation combined with least-privilege service identities
A single flat network with shared administrator credentials
Disabling all internal monitoring
Using one global encryption key for every host

text: Why should an organization preserve a forensic image before making extensive cleanup changes?
choices: Cleanup always improves evidentiary accuracy
Preservation supports later analysis of the original state and evidence
Forensic images automatically identify the attacker
It prevents the need for containment

text: What is the key trust assumption behind a public-key certificate authority?
choices: The authority can recover every private key from a certificate
The authority encrypts all application traffic itself
Clients trust the authority to bind a public key to an identity after validation
The authority guarantees the certificate holder's software is secure

text: What is the most accurate relationship between authentication and authorization in a secure API?
choices: Authorization identifies the caller; authentication checks the database schema
They are interchangeable names for encryption
Authentication is needed only after an action is completed
Authentication identifies the caller; authorization checks whether that caller may perform the requested action
